question: How does a piece under forty seconds still have two parts?
intro: The shortest piece in this recording is a chase: sforzando, then piano, then a flurry of staccato semiquavers, over and over. The second part begins with the same gesture, so the structure is easy to hear.

sections.label: B · second part: slurred contrast, then the gesture returns
sections.mNote: aligned order repeats bars 9–19, then the second ending

cues.title: A sforzando, then a scurry
cues.text: Two beats to the bar in B minor. Each strong bar opens with a note marked sfp — loud, then at once soft — and the right hand scampers away in staccato semiquavers with accents, over detached left-hand chords. By the report’s onset count this is the densest of the thirteen pieces.
cues.evidence: First edition p. 6 (IMSLP #03060): 2/4, sfp at the head of alternate bars, accents on the semiquaver groups, detached left-hand chords. The report counts 5.0 onsets per second at 0:00–0:05, the highest density of the thirteen pieces, and reads B minor (r = 0.79).
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The second part begins
cues.text: After eight bars and a double bar, the second part opens near 0:08 with the same sfp gesture and descending staccato lines. About four seconds later it turns to slurred, sustained notes and a rising chromatic run before the gesture returns. The provisional alignment follows the repeat, so the part is heard twice.
cues.evidence: Provisional alignment (docs/assets/data/schumann-kinderszenen-blind-mans-buff/score.json): bar 9 at 8.5 s, bar 13 at 12.7 s, bar 9 again at 21.5 s and the second ending, bar 21, at 33.4 s; performed order 1–20, 9–19, 21, 32 bars, no aural review. The report’s novelty 1.00 at 0:12 is a separate contrast inside the part (the slurred bars from bar 13), not the start of bar 9. Score p. 6 and the Mutopia transcription (SchumannOp15No03.ly): double bar after bar 8, sfp, slurred sustained notes, a chromatic run, repeat sign with two endings. The printed mark is crotchet = 138 (p. 6, enlarged scan).
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: The piece that closed a programme
cues.text: On 18 January 1853 Clara’s half-sister Marie Wieck played six of the pieces in Dresden. She took Hasche-Mann out of its printed place and used it as an effective finale. Schumann had given her the autograph of No. 1 in 1847.
cues.evidence: Zwickau catalogue 175 Jahre Kinderszenen, item 15 (programme, Cosel-Palais, Dresden, 18 January 1853, six pieces, Hasche-Mann used as the closing piece) and item 5 (the 1847 dedication to Marie Wieck).

transitions.title: The same sforzando opens the second part
transitions.how: The first eight bars end on a double bar and the second part starts again with the sfp opening, so the ear hears a new departure from familiar material. The staccato semiquavers continue at first; slurred, sustained notes and a rising chromatic run then supply the contrast, before the sfp gesture comes back to close the part.
transitions.evidence: Provisional alignment: bar 9 at 8.5 s and bar 13 at 12.7 s. Report: novelty 1.00 at 0:12, the strongest boundary in the recording, which marks the slurred contrast inside the part rather than the start of bar 9; the middle windows (0:15–0:25) are the loudest. Score p. 6: double bar after the first eight bars, sfp at the first bar of the second part, then slurred and sustained notes and a chromatic run.

composer.epithet: His music lets remembered fragments, concealed names and competing inner voices interrupt the forms that contain them.
facts: Piano with Friedrich Wieck; composition with Heinrich Dorn; extensive private study of Bach and Beethoven
Co-founder of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1834; editor until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
Leipzig Conservatoire teacher; municipal music director, Düsseldorf, 1850–53
composer.background:
Schumann grew up in Zwickau, where his father August was a bookseller and publisher. Reading and music developed together: Jean Paul’s novels, with their interruptions, doubles and changes of narrative voice, mattered alongside piano lessons. Sent to Leipzig to study law in 1828, he spent more time on music and literature; a period in Heidelberg did not reconcile him to a legal career. He returned to Leipzig to study piano seriously with Friedrich Wieck. Wieck’s daughter Clara, already performing publicly as a child, gave him an immediate example of the professional discipline he hoped to acquire.

A persistent problem with his right hand ended the prospect of a virtuoso career. The familiar account of a finger-strengthening device leaves the injury’s medical cause uncertain. Composition and criticism became his principal occupations. The early published piano works already had distinct literary and formal premises: the Abegg Variations derive a theme from letters, while Papillons relates its dances to the masked-ball ending of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The miniatures’ sudden juxtapositions recreate the experience of a narrative changing speakers and levels.
